name: quest-ai-runner library
description: A domain-free Python library: a bounded plan, gather, re-plan, answer loop that escalates to a deep runner when real work is needed (the core), a task executor that polls Quest, claims, runs, escalates and reports (the runner), and reference adapters for retrieval, model providers, cards, vectors, web research and deep runners, all wired by one configuration per lane and each swappable part chosen by metric.
advantages: One engine for chat and scheduled work; grounded in the consumer's sources; escalation built in; open source and reusable outside Quest; every part measured and swappable.
disadvantages: A large codebase to maintain; chat answer quality is currently weak on the cheapest model; some parts are measured only offline; consumers must keep adapters in step with the library.

name: Per-consumer worker
description: Each product writes its own worker and chat backend around a model vendor's API.
advantages: Fits its one product exactly; no shared-library coordination.
disadvantages: The plumbing is rebuilt and drifts per product (the history that led to QAR); improvements do not travel; chat and tasks diverge.

name: Agent framework with Quest glue
description: Build the engine from a general framework (LangGraph, CrewAI, an agent SDK) and add Quest grounding, escalation and the executor as glue.
advantages: Mature building blocks, community and tooling; less code of our own for the loop.
disadvantages: Grounding, scope containment, escalation, the executor and measured selection still have to be built; framework churn becomes a dependency risk.

name: Deep runner only
description: Hand every task straight to a coding agent such as Claude Code with the person's material available, with no routing or answering loop in front.
advantages: Strong at real multi-step work; very little engine code.
disadvantages: Slow and costly for simple questions; weaker grounding in Quest's own state; escalation and scope still need building; one vendor dependency.

name: Full planner decision
description: The orchestrator's own planner makes one planning call and its decision is the route. The call sees the message and a quest view and can return a tool with arguments, a deep brief, a confirm or a clarify. Only the planning step runs in the measured arm; nothing is executed.
advantages: Returns a real decision with arguments, confirm and clarify handling, and the context to brief a deep run or ground an answer. It is what production uses, so the measurement is of the live behaviour. Selected because: core/orchestrator_planning.py (PLANNER_PROFILES). A QAR lane runs the pre-route stage first (core/pre_route.py, owned by operate-a-quest, whose default is pre_route) and this planner decides every message the pre-route does not settle; quest-backend passes no pre-router, so Quest chat runs the planner alone
disadvantages: Every message pays for a planning call even when the request is plainly a simple tool use. Its rubric is long and has shown specific misses, such as sending a paraphrased state update to the wrong route and not confirming a mass destructive request.

name: Cheap pre-route in front of the planner
description: A small first model call names the route and, for a plain reversible create or find, the tool calls. It settles the turn only when it is sure and every call is on the direct-tool list with no confirming argument; every other message falls through to the same planner. The arm counts both calls where both ran.
advantages: Clear, safe requests can skip the heavy planning call, and a failed or unparsable pre-route costs nothing because the planner then decides. Destructive or ambiguous requests are never settled early.
disadvantages: Where the pre-route does not settle the message, the turn pays for two calls instead of one. On the measured cases it matches the planner on routing without being cheaper, so the extra stage has not been shown to earn its place on routing alone.

name: Unchecked single-prompt router
description: The pre-route is used alone with no planner behind it: one small model call returns a label, an optional set of tool calls and a sure flag, and whatever it says is the answer. It is an ablation that shows what the cheap call does when nothing checks it.
advantages: Cheapest model-based option: one small call and no planning scaffold. It scores well on labels, so it is a useful ceiling for how much a bare classifier can do.
disadvantages: It returns a label and tool calls, not a decision, so it cannot gather evidence, brief a deep run or ground an answer. It cannot express a confirm with a reason or recover from its own ambiguity, so it is ranked but never a candidate to replace the planner. Returns a label and tool calls, not a decision: it cannot gather evidence, brief a deep run or ground an answer, so it is ranked and never a candidate.

name: Keyword rules floor
description: Hand-written regular expressions map message wording to a route and tool with no model call: deep-work words send to deep, a few phrasings map to named tools, negations such as do not save map to answer, and the rest are answers. It is the baseline any model-based router must beat to justify its cost.
advantages: Free, instant, deterministic and easy to audit, and it makes a meaningful floor for judging whether a model call earns its cost.
disadvantages: It cannot fill arguments, handle multi-step requests, paraphrase or negation beyond its patterns, or confirm a destructive ask. Each new phrasing needs a new rule, so coverage decays as users word things differently.

name: Live chat on a disposable world
description: Drives the real in-app chat end to end on a disposable development account, running each case in a fresh conversation and restoring the world afterwards. Hard deterministic pre-checks run first, then a model judge scores the transcript against the case rubric and named pivot facts. It counts model calls and tokens when run in process.
advantages: Measures the true behaviour of the shipped brain on realistic data, including routing and side effects, and records the judge's reasons per case so failures can be read. Selected because: the Quest AI chat in the app, which runs this checkout's brain (core/orchestrator.py); the dev arm drives it end to end
disadvantages: Expensive, since a case is many model calls, and slow. It needs a development backend and a built world, the judge is not calibrated against human verdicts, and a small sample is noisy enough that one case can pass and then fail.

name: Offline metric validity check
description: No Quest and no model: for each case it validates the case against the dataset schema, checks that the deterministic pre-checks accept a reference reply built from the case's own expected phrases, and checks that they reject an empty reply. It proves the scoring is able to tell a good reply from none.
advantages: Free and deterministic, catches broken or vacuous cases before any spend, and keeps the offline suite green when no development account exists.
disadvantages: It says nothing about how well the chat actually answers. Its reference reply is derived from the case itself, so it cannot reveal a rubric that is wrong or too easy.

name: Planner-only orchestration
description: The whole brain handles the turn: the planner decides, the tool runs through the registry and a reply is composed, with the deep runner disabled so deep requests come back unexecuted. A fresh orchestrator and scratch corpus are built per case so no case sees another's turns.
advantages: Every message gets the full planning treatment, including reads, confirms and clarifies, so it is the most capable path and the reference for quality.
disadvantages: Pays for a planning call even on a plain create. Simple requests take more turns and tokens than they need.

name: Brain with a settling pre-route
description: The same brain with the pre-route selection on: a small first call may settle a clear, sure request for a direct tool before the planner runs, and every other message goes to the planner unchanged. Answers, reads, confirms and deep work are the planner's.
advantages: Clear requests finish with fewer planner turns, and because anything unsure or guarded falls through, it was never worse on quality than the planner alone.
disadvantages: The saving is smaller than the margin a sampled run can resolve, so it is a tie and not a proven win. A wrongly sure pre-route could write something the planner would have questioned, which the direct-tool list and confirm guard must prevent.

name: Direct tool-call ablation
description: One model call is given the quest record and the tool schemas and returns the tool calls as JSON, which the registry then executes. There is no planner and no answer step, so it is the upper bound on what the direct path alone can do for a plain edit.
advantages: The cheapest model path: a single call, no scaffolding. It shows how far plain edits can go without a planner.
disadvantages: It cannot read, answer, confirm or start a deep run, and it struggles with multi-step or ambiguous requests. It trusts one unchecked call to write, so it is not a replacement for the brain. Cheaper but cannot carry out multi-step or ambiguous requests.

name: Planner alone
description: The planner alone: the pre-route stage never looks and never settles a message, so every message goes to the planner. Costs no extra call.
advantages: Nothing extra to go wrong: no first call to fail or to settle a request wrongly.
disadvantages: Every clear request still pays for a planner turn.

name: Pre-route stage
description: The core pre-route module: a small model call returns a route, tool calls and a sure flag as JSON. The turn is settled only when the route is tool, it is sure, every call is on the direct-tool list and no argument confirms something; any failure or unparsable reply returns nothing so the planner decides.
advantages: Fails safe by construction: an error, a missing provider or an unsure answer costs only the one small call and never blocks the planner. It names no organisation or database, so any host can supply its own tool names. Selected because: TIE, kept by the stated reason: the pre-route and the planner alone pass the same cases at token spend inside the leaderboard's tolerance for sampled runs, so the metric does not choose; core/selection_table.py operate-a-quest (default pre_route; RunnerConfig.selections overrides) keeps the pre-route because it was never worse and settles clear requests with fewer planner turns. This row is the one owner of core/pre_route.py: a QAR lane runs the pre-route first and then the route-a-message planner; quest-backend passes no pre-router and runs the planner alone, unchanged
disadvantages: It adds a call before the planner on every message it does not settle. Its safety depends on the host flagging only genuinely safe tools as direct.

name: Local file tree reader
description: Reads and greps files under one configured root using only regular expressions and directory walking, with no shell. It resolves paths through the shared containment check, skips secret-like, binary and oversize files, and returns partial hits within a wall-clock grep budget.
advantages: Fast, dependency-free and strictly read-only, with a hard boundary that the write side shares, so there is one implementation of containment.
disadvantages: Keyword and regex only, so a paraphrase misses. Huge trees return partial hits when the time budget runs out.

name: Cached live-database reader
description: Serves structured queries over a consumer-supplied fetch function through a short-lived in-memory cache keyed on collection and canonical filter. It is thread-safe so the planner's parallel reads do not hammer the store, and nothing is synced to disk.
advantages: Reads live data where it lives, with cheap repeated reads inside the window and no sync job to keep fresh.
disadvantages: Data can be stale for the length of the cache window. It maps read and grep onto queries only where that makes sense, otherwise returning an unsupported observation.

name: Parallel multi-source composite
description: Runs a list of member adapters in separate threads and merges the results: reads grouped by source and path, searches deduplicated, queries combined with source attribution, and discovery merged. For named reads it tries each member and keeps the first non-error answer.
advantages: A single adapter slot reaches every source, and one slow or failing member does not stop the others. Source attribution lets the planner cite where evidence came from. Selected because: RunnerConfig.retrieval (config_source_builders)
disadvantages: Unscoped searches are broadcast to every member, which costs more when a member is remote or paid. Merge rules are simple, so ranking across sources is not relevance-aware.

name: MCP server reader
description: Maps the discovery and read surface onto one MCP server: resources list and read for sources and sections, tools list and describe for operations, and tool calls for queries gated by an explicit allowlist. Every name is prefixed with an alias so servers never collide.
advantages: Reaches any MCP-speaking system without bespoke code, and the allowlist keeps a tool it was not granted from ever being called.
disadvantages: Search is delegated to the server so its quality varies, and plain regex search is not supported. It is read-only by design, so mutations need the separate write adapter.

name: Remote file server reader
description: Reads files on another machine through a file-serving endpoint using the planner's ordinary file vocabulary, namespaced by alias. It refuses names without its alias before any network call, does not follow redirects, caps response size and never leaks the access token in errors.
advantages: Extends the same read vocabulary to other machines with safe failure and no credential leakage, and search results can be pasted straight into a read.
disadvantages: Every search costs a network round trip and so must be scoped. It depends on the remote server being reachable and, like the local reader, matches by pattern rather than meaning.

name: Notion database reader
description: A read-only adapter over a configured set of Notion databases: list them, query rows with simple filters, read a page's properties and bounded block text, and search across rows. Auth is injected, only configured databases may be read, and only reads can be sent.
advantages: Two locks make it incapable of writing, and it grounds answers in structured team records the other sources do not hold.
disadvantages: Locates rows by title and properties rather than body text, so content inside a page is hard to find. It depends on a pinned API version and the integration's access.

name: Drive document reader
description: Lists folders and reads file text from a workspace drive (documents, sheets, PDFs, plain text) through the standard retrieval surface, with injected auth and lazy PDF support. Unsupported types and permission errors return error observations.
advantages: Brings shared documents into the planner's reach without copying them, and failures never break the loop.
disadvantages: Drive offers no search here, so the policy is to list and read, which scales poorly on large folders. PDF text depends on an optional package.

name: Chat conversation reader
description: Lists spaces, pulls recent messages and groups them into conversations by thread or space, exposing them through read, search and query, with optional pre-flight assembly. Auth is injected and failures come back as error observations.
advantages: Lets answers draw on discussion that never reached a document, and supports incremental fetch of messages since a point in time.
disadvantages: Chat is noisy, so relevance depends on good scoping, and it needs a delegated-access service identity. Reading is bounded by what the credential may see.

name: Quest API context reader
description: Queries the Quest backend for goal metadata, notes, related goals, task history, decisions and reflections, and skips Quest queries when a task is local-only. It is designed to sit inside the composite beside file and database adapters.
advantages: Gives the planner the product's own structured context, including cross-environment discovery, in one source.
disadvantages: It is keyed by goal and quest identifiers rather than by a free-text question, so it cannot be ranked on question-driven retrieval and is pinned by decision tests instead. Keyed by goal and quest ids against the Quest API, not by a question, so it cannot be driven offline.

name: Snippet-first research with page extraction
description: The planner-facing adapter: concurrent multi-query search deduplicated by address into one terse observation, plus a focused page fetch that extracts main text, keeps only passages relevant to a focus phrase and caps the result. Everything is cached and a hosted fallback can read pages that resist direct extraction. Fetched addresses are checked against private targets.
advantages: Keeps prompt cost low and answers citable, repeats are free, and safe fetching and clean failure make it suitable as the default. Selected because: config_retrieval web_research wiring (QAR_WEB_SEARCH_*)
disadvantages: Quality is bounded by the chosen backend and a relevance heuristic. Pages built on scripts or behind blocks may need the fallback, and cached results can be stale.

name: Single-vendor retrieval-style search
description: A retrieval adapter that queries one search vendor over plain HTTP and returns the top pages as a synthesised result through the query surface. It is graceful, returning error observations for a missing key or unreachable endpoint.
advantages: Simple and dependency-free, with a clear configuration of key and result count.
disadvantages: Tied to one vendor and one key, with no fallback, no focused page extraction and none of the shared caching and budget handling.

name: Model-native search
description: A retrieval adapter that uses the configured model provider's built-in search tool or grounding, so any runner with a model key can search the web with no extra setup, through the same surface as the dedicated adapter.
advantages: Key-free beyond the model key, so it is the easiest default to switch on.
disadvantages: Search spend and latency are tied to model calls and priced per grounded prompt, results are less controllable than a dedicated search API, and it fails where the provider has no such tool.

name: Pluggable search backends with fallback
description: Several search vendors and a self-hosted option sit behind one small search-backend protocol with an injectable HTTP callable, and a selector picks one or builds a fallback chain from environment settings, with grounded model search as the key-light fallback.
advantages: Swapping or chaining vendors is configuration, outages degrade to the next backend, and offline tests can prove identical handling for every vendor.
disadvantages: Vendors differ in cost and result shape, and only the configured ones have been measured live. The offline payloads are written in each vendor's shape rather than recorded, so they show handling, not relevance. Not measured live: the backend is not configured in the environment.

name: Brave search backend
description: A search backend over the Brave Search API with an injectable HTTP callable.
advantages: Independent index; swapped in or chained by configuration.
disadvantages: Needs an API key and a paid or rate-limited plan. Not measured live: the backend is not configured in the environment.

name: Tavily search backend
description: A search backend over the Tavily API with an injectable HTTP callable.
advantages: Returns extracted content with results; swapped in or chained by configuration.
disadvantages: Needs an API key and a plan. Not measured live: the backend is not configured in the environment.

name: SearXNG search backend
description: A search backend over a self-hosted SearXNG instance with an injectable HTTP callable.
advantages: No vendor key and full control of the sources.
disadvantages: Needs an instance to run and keep up. Not measured live: the backend is not configured in the environment.

name: Gemini grounded search backend
description: Searches via Gemini's native Google Search grounding tool (google.genai) with its own client and resolves redirect links to the real source pages.
advantages: Key-light fallback that works whichever provider runs the planner; citations point at the actual page.
disadvantages: Depends on one vendor's grounding tool and on resolving redirects over the network.

name: Provider-native search backend
description: Wraps any model provider that exposes a web search method (query, model, max results).
advantages: No separate search vendor or key when the model provider already searches.
disadvantages: Quality and limits are those of the wrapped provider.

name: Anthropic SDK provider
description: The reference provider over the Anthropic SDK: a forced-structured planning call, a normal grounded completion, and a cached latest-first model list. Stable prompt layers become cacheable system blocks. The SDK is imported lazily.
advantages: Forced tool choice gives reliable structured plans, and prompt caching cuts repeated-context cost.
disadvantages: Needs a paid API key and bills per token, and the library cannot load it where the SDK is absent.

name: Gemini provider
description: A provider over the Google genai SDK offering JSON-forced planning, answering with native system-instruction splitting of prompt layers, and a cached model list, with lazy import.
advantages: A cost-effective tier for cheap planning and answering, and it also supplies grounding for web search.
disadvantages: JSON-mode planning is less strictly enforced than forced tool choice, so malformed output needs parse-and-retry handling.

name: OpenAI provider
description: A provider over the OpenAI SDK with JSON-mode structured planning, ordinary answering and a cached model list, written with hooks so compatible vendors can subclass it.
advantages: One adapter covers the vendor and any compatible endpoint, which keeps additions small.
disadvantages: JSON-mode output must be parsed with retry, and tier bucketing relies on model identifier conventions.

name: DeepSeek provider
description: A thin subclass of the OpenAI-compatible provider pointed at the DeepSeek endpoint, registered only when its key is set, with thinking off by default. Its models are never auto-bucketed into tiers, so a deployment opts in by pinning.
advantages: Low-cost option that needs almost no new code, and opt-in tiering prevents surprise use.
disadvantages: Quality has been measured below the preferred cheap tier on routing, so it is a deliberate pin, not a default. Thinking mode is slower and costs more output.

name: Keyless command-line provider
description: Drives the local Claude command-line tool in print mode so planning and answering run on the operator's subscription login. Planning asks for only the decision JSON and parses leniently, and the spawned process has API credentials stripped from its environment.
advantages: No API key and no per-token billing, so a whole runner can operate on a subscription alone.
disadvantages: Spawning a process adds latency, the tool cannot force a tool choice, and tiers are limited to the model families the tool can run.

name: Prefix-routing multi-provider
description: Wraps a primary provider and a set of vendor providers, routes each call by model-name prefix, steps down a tier when a quota error occurs, and applies shared retry for transient errors. Callers see one provider.
advantages: Vendor and tier changes are configuration, and quota exhaustion degrades service instead of failing. It beats a single flat provider on the offline cases. Selected because: QAR_MODEL_BACKEND and ModelRegistry tiers
disadvantages: More moving parts and a per-call routing decision. Fallback hides a degraded tier unless logged, and price knowledge is input-only.

name: Single flat provider floor
description: A baseline in which every model name goes to one provider, a quota error is final, transient errors are not retried, the dry run counts input only and every model has the same price. It is the floor the multi-provider stack must beat.
advantages: Trivially simple and predictable, and it shows the value of each added capability by removal.
disadvantages: No resilience, no tier-aware cost, and one vendor outage stops everything.

name: Subprocess goal runner
description: Wraps any worker with the goal contract (composing the goal and brief, enforcing the turn bound, reading met versus limit) and provides the reference worker that spawns headless Claude Code with a goal directive. Working directory, binary, model and preamble are configuration, and a periodic liveness review can stop a stalled run.
advantages: Full autonomy for open-ended work, the simplest way to run, and the common contract keeps outcomes uniform. Selected because: config_resolvers.resolve_deep_runner_ladder
disadvantages: A fresh process per attempt throws away gathered context and is slow and costly for small edits. Nothing can reach it mid-run, so new user input only lands on the next attempt (the stream_json runner is the alternative that can be steered).

name: Agent-protocol deep runner
description: An opt-in alternative worker that holds a two-way session with an agent over the Agent Client Protocol, so a message can be injected into the turn that is running through a steering poll or a direct call. It never raises and turns a missing package, old runtime or wedged turn into a clear unmet result.
advantages: Mid-run steering, so late user input need not wait for the next attempt, with typed protocol instead of parsed command-line output.
disadvantages: Extra dependencies and a recent Node runtime are needed, there is more to configure, and it buys nothing when no one steers.

name: One-call fast file editor
description: Hands the model the context already gathered plus the current content of candidate files, asks for the edit in one call, and applies it in process through the file writer. It can touch only files already in context, does nothing when no candidate is found, and retries once with a diagnostic if a search block fails to match.
advantages: Roughly one round trip instead of an agent session, no startup, and a strict blast radius, with escalation as the safe default.
disadvantages: Limited to bounded edits to known files, and a weak edit relies on the goal loop's verifier to notice and escalate.

name: One-call MCP operation runner
description: Mirrors the fast editor for named operations: with forced structured output the model picks at most one writable operation from the writer's own catalogue and its arguments, the writer executes it, and a decline falls through to the next rung. It is reachable only through the deep ladder.
advantages: Cheap single call for a governed mutation, and an explicit decline value keeps it from guessing.
disadvantages: Can do only one operation and only those allow-listed, so multi-step or unlisted work escalates.

name: Subprocess runner scenarios
description: The selected reference worker driven through the common run entry with the process launch replaced by a scripted peer (exit code, output, stderr, missing binary, crash). Only the process edge is faked, and the way each outcome is reported is compared.
advantages: Zero model cost, repeatable, and exercises the real reporting code path.
disadvantages: Produces no tokens or dollars, so it cannot show cost per success, and it does not exercise real worker behaviour.

name: Agent-protocol runner scenarios
description: The opt-in protocol worker driven through the same run entry, with its single connection seam replaced by a scripted session (message chunks, a stop reason, a missing agent, a crash). The same scenarios allow a like-for-like comparison with the subprocess runner.
advantages: Shows that both workers report outcomes identically, at no model cost.
disadvantages: A scripted session cannot reveal real steering behaviour, latency or cost, and the opt-in extra must be installed to run it.

name: Goal contract rules check
description: Calls the deterministic rules of the done-standard directly: review parsing, liveness helpers, escalation, resume and envelope markers, prompt composition, met-versus-limit normalisation, and the orchestrator goal loop with a scripted runner and verifier, with the environment pinned.
advantages: Covers the logic every runner shares, with no model calls and no worker started.
disadvantages: Tests the contract, not any worker's ability to do the job, and relies on scripted runners that follow the cases.

name: Persistent stream-json runner
description: Holds one live Claude Code session per run over its stream-json input and output, so the person can steer, stop or pause while it works. A message is claimed only at the moment it is written to the session, so it arrives once and only for its own run; the model's replay of it marks it seen. A stop sends an interrupt and keeps the session, and a worker that ignores it is terminated and then killed after a grace period. A pause releases the process and resumes later on the same session. It keeps the live progress stream, resume, the subscription login, the usage-limit wait and the liveness review, and hands the run to the one-shot runner when the installed Claude Code cannot report an interrupt.
advantages: A message reaches the worker's next step within seconds instead of after the whole run, a stop takes effect at once and keeps finished work, a pause costs no memory while it waits, and a message that was written but not confirmed seen is handed back instead of being lost.
disadvantages: Not measured against live runs yet, so it is selected by nobody. It needs a Claude Code recent enough to answer an interrupt, a long-lived process per active run on a shared host, and its replay of a message is matched by text. The priority flag that should move work to the background did not do so in the probe, so only the default priority is used.

name: Production liveness review in the goal runner
description: The runner's liveness check: it first detects a usage limit from the session file, skips the model when a subagent is in flight, then sends the review prompt with elapsed time, idle time and log tail to a one-shot command-line model call and parses the verdict. Any failure to reach or read the reviewer means keep running.
advantages: Judges the situation rather than matching words, and fails open so work is protected.
disadvantages: Each review costs a model call and depends on the command-line tool being present, and its judgement can vary between runs.

name: Live model reviewer arm
description: Fills the production review prompt exactly as the runner does, sends it through the same one-shot call and reads it with the production parser, scored against hand-labelled logs. It needs the command-line tool and a small call per log.
advantages: Measures the shipped reviewer itself, including its prompt and parser, with false stops counted separately. Selected because: core/goal_runner.py SubprocessGoalRunner._review_liveness (the review prompt and parser, run through claude -p at the review model)
disadvantages: Costs model calls, cannot run where the tool is absent, and the labelled set is small without held-out real-run logs.

name: Keyword and threshold rule floor
description: A baseline decides from fixed signals: stop on a named usage or credit limit, on text saying the worker is blocked on a person, on the same command repeated, or on a long idle with no sign of a machine at work. Everything else keeps running.
advantages: Free, instant and explainable, and a fair floor a model reviewer must match.
disadvantages: Written with the cases in view, so its score is optimistic, and keyword lists miss new phrasings and cannot read an unfamiliar log. Idle thresholds are blunt.

name: Contained backed-up writer
description: Resolves every path through the same containment function the reader uses, refuses secret-like names, binary files and oversize payloads, copies the previous content to a backup outside the corpus before replacing it, and returns a result value instead of raising.
advantages: One shared boundary, small enough to audit, with recoverability that does not depend on version control. Selected because: RunnerConfig.file_writer
disadvantages: Fixed deny lists can miss unusual names, concurrent writers are unhandled, and a failed backup makes the write refuse.

name: Scratch-tree boundary check
description: Drives the production writer on temporary trees with an outside file as a sentinel, and observes whether the write succeeded, whether the outside stayed intact, the final content and whether a backup was kept.
advantages: Offline and exact, proving the boundary with real file operations and no mocks beyond the directories.
disadvantages: Covers the cases written down only, and does not test concurrency or very large trees.

name: MCP operation writer
description: Lists the allow-listed subset of a server's tools as writable operations and executes one by name through the client, refusing anything off the allowlist before the network, with alias namespacing and an audit detail on every result.
advantages: Strong guard and full auditability for each attempt, sharing a connection with the read adapter while keeping a separate policy. Selected because: config_resolvers.resolve_mcp_write_runners
disadvantages: Allowlist hygiene is on the host, and a call is not idempotent, so a retry after an ambiguous failure could repeat a mutation.

name: Fake-client allowlist check
description: Runs the production writer against a fake client at the process edge to check listing, exact tool and arguments once, aliased and bare names, refusals with zero calls, server error and dead connection.
advantages: Offline, fast and precise about what reached the client.
disadvantages: A fake client cannot show how real servers behave, so protocol quirks are untested.

name: Decision-request sink
description: Adapts the Quest client into the escalation port: it resolves an assignee (explicit, then default, then the quest owner), refuses to file an unaddressed ask, applies a deadline default, and creates a hold-default team decision request whose identifier it returns.
advantages: Never files an ask nobody will see, and puts decisions where the team already works. Selected because: RunnerConfig.escalation (defaults to QuestDecisionSink)
disadvantages: Tied to one backend's decision model, and a missing owner or backend failure surfaces as an error rather than a quiet fallback.

name: Fake-backend delivery check
description: Runs the production sink against an in-memory fake client, checking the assignee fallback chain, kind, default, deadline, review link, team routing, repeated asks and backend failure.
advantages: Offline and exact about what was filed and to whom.
disadvantages: Scores delivery and detail only, not whether the brain chose to escalate, and the fake cannot show real backend behaviour.

name: Stream, milestone and fan-out sinks
description: The stream sink forwards every event to the consumer's stream, the milestone sink forwards only the always-surfacing event types to named callbacks, and the fan-out sink sends live events to both and supports detaching the live side. A failing forward or callback never breaks the run.
advantages: Policy lives in one place so every consumer inherits it, and failures in a consumer cannot stop the work. Selected because: Mode selects StreamSink or MilestoneSink
disadvantages: Policy is fixed by event type, so a consumer wanting a different split must write a sink, and swallowed failures can hide a dead stream.

name: Milestone sink
description: A background sink that surfaces only result, decision, milestone, context and done events to named callbacks.
advantages: A quiet default for background work: the person sees outcomes and decisions only.
disadvantages: A consumer wanting a different split must write a sink.

name: Sink policy cases
description: Builds the production sinks and feeds them event sequences for live, background, handoff and broken-stream cases, recording what each surfaced.
advantages: Offline and deterministic, and exercises the real sinks, including the failure paths.
disadvantages: Scores the sinks only; it cannot say whether the orchestrator emits the right events.

name: Local session-file conversation store
description: Reads local Claude session files and answers related-conversation queries in two stages: a cached per-file digest ranks every file by term relevance with a small recency boost and a recency floor, then only a capped shortlist is fully parsed, scope-filtered and sampled into slices. Parsed conversations sit in a small least-recently-used cache validated by modification time and size.
advantages: Needs no database or network, scales its cost with a fixed cap rather than history size, and keeps old but relevant conversations reachable. Degrades to relevance-only when a filter matches nothing and says so. Selected because: RunnerConfig.conversation_store
disadvantages: Term-based ranking cannot bridge a paraphrase that shares no words with the old thread. Only files on one host are visible, and only the related-slices path is exercised by the evaluation, not the current-slice path or other backends.

name: Field-weighted keyword arm
description: Runs the production keyword store over one deterministic card per file (name, symbols, docstring summary), scoring task tokens with field-weighted inverse document frequency and returning the files of the ranked cards, with the confidence gate off so a ranking always comes back.
advantages: No model, no network, no embedder; strong on exact identifiers and symptoms and the best cheap arm in the measured set. Is the live keyword path, so it tracks production.
disadvantages: Blind to meaning: a paraphrase sharing no rare word with a card misses. Quality depends on docstrings being present and informative.

name: Docstring ablation of the keyword arm
description: The same keyword store with each card's summary and description blanked so only path tokens and symbol names remain. It is an ablation that measures how much the orientation text contributes, not a way anyone would deploy.
advantages: Shows cleanly that docstring text matters, and needs no extra data. Cheapest possible card.
disadvantages: Clearly worse than the full arm on paraphrase and hard tasks; relies on good file and symbol naming. Not a candidate for production.

name: Blind text-search floor
description: Counts how many distinct task tokens appear anywhere in each source file and ranks by that count, with no cards, docstrings or index. It is the floor any context layer must beat to justify existing.
advantages: Trivial, needs no preparation, and finds literal strings the card text may not mention.
disadvantages: Common words swamp the signal, long files win by accident, and it reads every file per task so it scales poorly. It was the weakest arm.

name: Plain cosine semantic baseline
description: Embeds each file card with a small local embedder using the same embed text as production and ranks by cosine similarity to the embedded task. It reimplements the ranking rather than wrapping the live vector assembler, so it is a baseline for the semantic idea, not a measurement of the live class.
advantages: Catches paraphrase and intent that keywords miss, and is competitive on the grown task set. Runs offline with a local model.
disadvantages: Misses exact identifiers that the keyword arm nails, needs an embedder, and uses a small local embedding rather than the production one, so the result is only indicative.

name: Keyword plus vector fusion (measured live class)
description: Drives the real hybrid assembler offline: the live keyword store and the live vector assembler over an in-memory store are run together and fused by reciprocal rank with the vector rank at reduced weight, each arm capped, and read at the strict top few. Only the consolidating model pass is switched off.
advantages: Measures the class that production actually selects, and it is the only arm that can recover a paraphrase while keeping keyword precision on identifiers.
disadvantages: On the grown proxy it only ties the keyword arm on strict top few, so its extra cost (embedding, a second arm, more latency) has no measured rank benefit yet. The embedder and tasks are not production.

name: Card-file keyword store
description: Stores each context card as a JSON document through a pluggable card repository and selects cards by field-weighted keyword overlap with a confidence gate. It checks each pinned file's hash and modification time to flag stale cards, renders fresh cards with typed references (files, collections, conversations) resolved at read time, and learns by updating cards after runs.
advantages: Standard library only, deterministic and cheap, with stable render order and usage-aware ordering inside a card. Keeps cards fresh and lets a consumer own protected fields.
disadvantages: Keyword recall only, so paraphrases miss when the gate is strict and over-select when it is open. Learning quality depends on the updater model and on the sources the cards point to.

name: Semantic card retrieval
description: Searches a vector store with the task text and optionally several model-generated queries in parallel, optionally has a model review the hits, applies a raw-similarity confidence floor so an unrelated query returns nothing, resolves card references fresh, and renders survivors in a stable order by card id so prompt caches stay valid.
advantages: Finds paraphrased and conceptual matches, abstains on unrelated queries, and works with any vector store behind the protocol.
disadvantages: Needs an embedder and index, the agentic variants add model calls and latency, and a card is embedded from its beginning so facts deep inside a long card can be missed.

name: Parallel keyword and vector fusion
description: Runs the keyword and vector assemblers in parallel, fuses their cards by reciprocal rank into one labelled view, honours a call deadline by returning the finished arm as a partial result, and can run a consolidating model pass to prefer previously useful items. If both arms are empty it returns nothing so the caller proceeds plainly.
advantages: Highest recall of the live options, tolerant of one arm failing or being slow, and keeps both stores learning through shared record calls. Selected because: config.resolve_context_assembler (hybrid when QAR_VECTOR_STORE is set)
disadvantages: More moving parts and cost than either arm, and the benefit over the keyword arm alone is not yet demonstrated. The union can inflate the prompt if caps are loose.

name: Exact-content BM25 arm
description: Indexes the actual text of files in a corpus with BM25, refreshing only files whose hash changed, and optionally has a model generate several keyword queries that are searched in parallel and merged by best score per path.
advantages: Finds rare identifiers and exact phrases that neither card summaries nor embeddings contain, and updates itself cheaply.
disadvantages: Needs an optional dependency and indexes whole file bodies, so memory and build time grow with the corpus. It matches words, not meaning, and is not part of the measured default path.

name: Per-agent preference wrapper
description: Wraps any inner assembler, prepends the learned context preferences of the agent identity handling the run, and after a run that really consulted sources pushes one concise, de-duplicated preference back to that agent's profile. It leaves persona and corrections to the library's other paths so nothing is doubled.
advantages: Captures that different agents lean on different sources, without polluting the shared card store, and degrades to no block on any failure.
disadvantages: Depends on an external profile service and on the current agent being known to the worker thread. It adds a fetch per call and can only reflect what runs actually read.

name: Ordered assembler composition
description: Calls each member assembler in order, concatenates their context views, merges card ids, stale lists, sources and metadata, keeps the first tier hint, isolates a failing member, and forwards record and card rendering to the members. It also provides the walker that finds a store of a given kind inside wrapped assemblers.
advantages: Lets unrelated sources be combined without a bespoke class, and one member failing never loses the others.
disadvantages: Does no ranking or de-duplication across members, so overlapping sources can repeat content and the order alone decides what leads.

name: Seeded keyword card-quality arm
description: Writes cards from a small world of learned tasks with a deterministic extractor (keywords, summary, typed collection references), reads them back through the real keyword store with its default confidence gate, and a stub resolver returns identifiable fresh rows. It measures the persisted-card path (selection, fresh resolution, no leak), not a model's learning of cards.
advantages: Offline and deterministic, with no model or network, and it tests the gate that prevents spraying unrelated cards.
disadvantages: A paraphrase that shares no rare word is not selected at all, and the extractor is not the real learner, so card writing quality is untested.

name: Open-gate ablation of the card-quality arm
description: The same seeded cards and real store with the confidence threshold at zero, as an older script had it. With no vector arm to filter, it selects a best-scoring card for any query, showing what the keyword arm does when it never abstains.
advantages: Never misses for lack of confidence, and documents why the gate exists.
disadvantages: Selects a card even for an unrelated query, so it leaks irrelevant context; it is a diagnostic, not a deployable setting.

name: Live learner plus hybrid store arm
description: Runs the real asynchronous card updater (a model call per learned task) into a vector-backed card repository, then assembles queries through a keyword store fused with a query-only vector arm using a similarity floor. It is the end-to-end outcome path, not yet run.
advantages: Tests the full learn-then-select loop including the model's card writing and the production backend recipe.
disadvantages: Needs a model backend, a vector client and an embedding key, spends tokens, is unrecorded, and its first run is expected to need shake-down.

name: Offline warm-hint builder
description: Builds the hint an agent would receive (the top few files from the keyword arm) and reports it as the answer, so the arm scores what the hint would contain without running an agent.
advantages: Zero model cost, and it isolates hint quality from agent behaviour.
disadvantages: Does not show that an agent actually finds files faster with the hint; it only shows the hint is right.

name: Agent without hint
description: Runs the coding agent headless in a copy of the repository with no hint and asks it to locate the file. It is the control for whether warm context helps.
advantages: A fair, real-world control on the same tasks.
disadvantages: Spends model tokens, needs the agent CLI, and is not recorded, so the control is unmeasured.

name: Agent with hint
description: Runs the same headless agent given the offline keyword hint, or a deliberately wrong hint on some cases, to test both the benefit and the harm of a bad hint.
advantages: Measures the real end effect the context layer is meant to have, including the cost of a misleading hint.
disadvantages: Spends tokens, needs the CLI, is not recorded, and results vary run to run.

name: Atomic JSON file repository
description: Stores one JSON file per card in a directory, writing through a temporary file and an atomic replace, and exposes a cheap change stamp from the newest modification time and file count so other processes' writes invalidate caches. Measured by the shared conformance scenarios against a temporary folder with a restart harness.
advantages: Simplest backend, no dependencies, easy to inspect and back up, crash-safe writes; fast and fully offline to measure, and the reference behaviour the other backends are compared with.
disadvantages: Single host only, no native search, and listing reads every file, which is slow at large volume; the conformance run cannot show behaviour of remote backends such as network failure or server-side paging.

name: Vector database repository
description: Stores each card as one point in a Qdrant collection, embedding it once at write time with a consumer-supplied embedder, with an optional scope payload filter so tenants cannot see each other's cards. It pages through the collection for listing and offers native card search. Measured by the same conformance scenarios on an embedded local folder with a deterministic hash embedder, closing the client on restart.
advantages: Combines persistence and semantic search without a separate index, supports tenant isolation, and runs embedded or against a server; the measurement exercises paging, restart and scope behaviour without any model or server.
disadvantages: Needs the optional dependency and an embedder, and writes cost an embedding. The server variant is not exercised by the evaluation, and a hash embedder says nothing about retrieval quality.

name: Hosted card API repository
description: Reads and writes cards through the host application's card API with a bearer key, choosing a private, team or organisation scope per call, resolving id collisions in favour of the write scope, and server-side embedding and search. Failures are logged loudly, counted and kept. Measured by the same conformance scenarios against an in-process fake of the documented card contract.
advantages: Shared across lanes and devices with server-enforced access, and no local embedding or index is needed; the measurement checks the client against the documented contract, including volume, paging and concurrent writers, without a live service. Selected because: QAR_CARDS_SCOPE and card store mounts
disadvantages: Depends on network and a running service, so latency and outages matter, and the evaluation uses a fake of the contract rather than the live service, so real server behaviour can still differ.

name: Qdrant-backed vector store
description: Embeds text with a pluggable or local embedder and stores it in one collection keyed by embedding dimension, with a hashed scope field filtered at search time. Sync compares stored fingerprints and re-embeds only changed or missing items, and optional capacity methods count and evict the oldest.
advantages: Runs embedded with no server or remotely at scale, isolates tenants without many collections, and keeps itself fresh with little cost. Selected because: QAR_VECTOR_STORE
disadvantages: A long card is embedded from its start only, so deep answers are missed. Embedded latency and the small local embedder are not production figures, and it has no second implementation to compare against.

name: Universal guidance provider
description: Merges file-based guidance cards with dynamic guidance from feedback and rep profiles, scores them by tags, keywords and optional vector similarity, optionally filters with a model, and returns the top few for injection. It re-reads dynamic sources each selection so new feedback appears at once.
advantages: One provider covers static policy and learned corrections, supports semantic selection, and picks up change without restart. Selected because: RunnerConfig.guidance_provider
disadvantages: Without a vector or model filter it has no relevance cut under the card limit, so unrelated rules can show. Model filtering adds latency and cost.

name: Live ledger and provider arm
description: Replays correction and turn steps through the real feedback ledger, run-account receipt and guidance writer, then runs a real orchestrator with the real provider and reads the guidance block from the planner prompt it sent. Only the model is scripted.
advantages: Tests the true loop end to end for recall and precision at no model cost, and was clearly best of the three arms.
disadvantages: Shares the live weakness on precision, and a scripted model says nothing about whether a real model obeys the guidance.

name: No-feedback floor
description: An assistant that hears corrections and forgets them: no later turn is shown anything, so it never leaks and never repeats.
advantages: Zero cost and perfect precision by construction, which isolates the value of the loop.
disadvantages: Recall is nil, so every correction must be made again; it is the worst arm on the repeat-correction rate.

name: Show-everything baseline
description: Remembers every correction verbatim and shows all of them on every later turn, with no ledger, no standing-versus-one-off distinction and no relevance.
advantages: Perfect recall and trivially simple, so it shows what the real loop must beat on precision.
disadvantages: One-off requests become permanent rules and unrelated rules crowd every prompt, growing the prompt without bound.

name: MCP gateway bridge transport
description: Wraps a generic MCP client to speak a small fixed set of gateway tools: long-poll for events to receive, send a message, and best-effort attachment fetch. It deliberately has no code path that responds to the gateway's own permission requests, clamps the poll timeout and tolerates key spelling drift.
advantages: Reuses a maintained gateway so many chat networks become channels without new code, and its small tool surface limits risk. Selected because: RunnerConfig.channel_transport
disadvantages: Depends on the gateway's availability and security posture and on guessed payload shapes. Only one channel family is covered.

name: Fake-gateway conformance arm
description: Drives the production channel with a fake MCP client injected at the process edge and records ids, texts, health, poll timeout, attachment sizes and whether only allowed tools were called.
advantages: Offline, fast and deterministic, with the real production class under test.
disadvantages: Proves agreement with the assumed wire shapes, not with a real gateway, until a recorded fixture exists.

name: Live recipe replay arm
description: The orchestrator with a recipe store and the real model: the first success teaches a recipe, and a later matching request replays the tool call before any context search through one fill-arguments call.
advantages: Measures the real cost and correctness benefit with a real model, changing only the recipe store against the baseline. Selected because: RunnerConfig.recipe_store
disadvantages: Needs the model CLI and spends tokens; built but not recorded, so the real-model result is missing.

name: Live planner-only baseline
description: The normal path with no recipe store: plan, search context, call the tool, reply, with one orchestrator for the whole run.
advantages: The correctness reference every recipe approach must match, and it needs no learning state.
disadvantages: Pays a full planning and search cost on every repeat; unrecorded for lack of an approved model run.

name: Offline recipe replay arm
description: The live orchestrator and live recipe store over a fake tool world with a deterministic rule model standing in for the model, so the replay engine (nominate, fill arguments, mutating guard, learning) is exercised with its real model-call count.
advantages: Offline, free and repeatable, and shows fewer model calls at the same pass rate.
disadvantages: The rule model is an optimistic ceiling written with the cases in view, so it does not show real model judgment.

name: Offline planner-only baseline
description: The same orchestrator, fake world and rule model with no recipe store, so every request takes the full path.
advantages: Gives the exact like-for-like count of model calls to compare against, at no cost.
disadvantages: Shares the rule model's optimism and so only checks parity and call count, not real behaviour.

name: Digest-driven overseer
description: Builds a capped compact digest of the run, makes one structured model call with a fixed prompt and tool schema, validates the answer against the five signals, and returns proceed on any error, non-object response or unknown signal.
advantages: Very low token cost, safe by default, and cannot distort a run without an explicit signal. Selected because: RunnerConfig.overseer
disadvantages: Quality rests on the digest keeping the right evidence and on a model deciding well, and the live signal match is unmeasured.

name: No-judgement digest probe
description: A floor arm that always returns no signal, so the scorer measures only whether the digest shows the evidence each label turns on.
advantages: Free, offline and isolates the digest from model judgment.
disadvantages: Says nothing about whether the model reads the evidence correctly.

name: Live overseer model arm
description: Calls the production overseer function against the real provider, one small call per scenario, and fails if the overseer degraded.
advantages: Measures actual signal correctness with the production prompt.
disadvantages: Needs a model backend and spend, and has not been recorded.

name: Content-hash fingerprint check
description: Pins a content hash plus modification time to each file when its card is written and recomputes the hash on query to see whether the file changed, using a modification-time fast path.
advantages: Exact for real content changes and catches deletes, and is the production check. Selected because: FileContextStore staleness check (_current_sha)
disadvantages: Trusts an edit that restores time and size, and hashing costs a read when it runs.

name: Timestamp-and-size baseline
description: Compares modification time and size per file before and after, with no hashing.
advantages: Nearly free and trivial, so it is a good floor.
disadvantages: Misses same-size edits with restored time, and falsely flags files that were only touched.

name: Live assembly-point driver
description: Drives the real planner prompt builder with a capture provider, plus the real autopilot batch composer, context-update block renderer and deep goal prompt composer, and reports size and duplicates for each fixture.
advantages: Measures what the live paths really produce with no model calls, and covers four assembly points. Selected because: live paths: Orchestrator._plan, autopilot_briefs.compose_batch_text, ContextUpdates.as_prompt_block, goal_runner_contract.compose_goal_prompt (fitted by core/prompt_budget.py)
disadvantages: Fixtures are synthetic filler, and budgets are partly policy, so it checks size, not whether the prompt holds the right content.

name: Production judges under a scripted provider
description: Calls the real overseer, reach-judge parser and block builder, quest ranker and sufficiency helpers with a scripted provider that returns fixed output or raises, so only the deterministic halves are exercised.
advantages: Fast, free and exact on the parts that must never fail, with failure injection. Selected because: core/reach_judge.py, core/quest_judge.py, core/overseer.py, core/sufficiency.py wired by core/orchestrator_judges.py
disadvantages: Compared against a trusting baseline only, and it says nothing about what the real models decide.

name: Production guard engines under test
description: Calls the real link guard with a fake fetch table, link extraction, an in-memory recipe store and the pure anticipation functions directly, with no model or network.
advantages: Deterministic and fast, and covers all three guards with the real code. Selected because: core/link_guard.py (build_link_guard), core/recipes.py, core/anticipation.py wired by config
disadvantages: Does not show live behaviour of replay through a real model or real network noise, which other solutions own.

name: Source interface with shared channel flags
description: Defines the source contract (a name and a collect call that must never raise) and a base class whose class-level flags decide how the engine treats each channel: relevance judgment, admission judgment, ask tracking and relaying. The live engine and concrete channels build on it, so the rules are declared per channel rather than hard-coded in the engine.
advantages: New channels slot in by declaring flags, with no engine change. The card-scoped versus user-scoped split is stated once, with the incident that motivated it. Selected because: fixed in code
disadvantages: The flags are trust-based: a channel author who sets one wrong silently changes what is tracked or judged. It defines the contract only, so it cannot show on its own that the offered set is correct.

name: Live engine over fake quest channels
description: Runs the real update engine with the real notes, goal-update and decision sources against a fake client, selecting which channels are watched per case and applying the engine's own first-look window and open-ask bounds. It reports the sorted offered ids and the ids needing a response, with no model calls.
advantages: Exercises the shipped code path end to end, deterministically and free, so any change to the rules shows up as an exact-set mismatch.
disadvantages: The cases restate rules the code already follows, so passing is a regression pin rather than proof the rules are right. External channels such as mail, documents and chat are not covered because they need real accounts.

name: File-backed feedback ledger
description: Keeps every tracked item in one small JSON document beside the lane's state, locked across threads and processes and written atomically, with a state machine of open, in progress, partially applied, needs reapplying and done. It exposes a two-method store seam so another store can replace the file, and offers standing rules to a guidance writer.
advantages: Needs no database, survives restarts, keeps the person's words intact, and the vocabulary and state machine are shared by any store behind the seam. Selected because: fixed in code
disadvantages: Whole-document read and replace does not scale to very large histories, and the file is single-host. Correctness of status rests on the run reporting its disposition honestly.

name: Ledger plus guidance bridge, end to end
description: Replays a script of corrections and turns through the real ledger, the real run-account recording, the real guidance card manager and provider, and a real orchestrator with a scripted model, then reads the guidance shown from the prompt the planner received. It measures whether a standing rule reappears and a one-time request does not.
advantages: Tests the whole loop as shipped rather than the pieces, with no model calls, and shows the exact guidance a later turn sees.
disadvantages: Its misses reflect guidance-selection precision more than storage fidelity, and the scripted model means real run wording is not tested.

name: No-memory floor
description: An assistant that hears a correction and forgets it, so no later turn is shown anything. It is the floor the loop must beat on how often a person has to repeat a correction.
advantages: Never leaks an irrelevant correction and costs nothing, so it marks the best possible precision and the worst possible recall.
disadvantages: Every correction must be repeated, which is the problem itself, and standing rules are never kept.

name: Remember-everything baseline
description: Stores every correction verbatim regardless of kind and shows all of them on every later turn, with no ledger, no split between standing and one-off, and no relevance step.
advantages: Perfect recall by construction and trivial to build, so it shows how much recall is available for free.
disadvantages: A one-time request becomes a permanent rule, unrelated rules crowd every prompt, and cost grows with the history.

name: Lexical-gated scoped file store
description: Keeps one small JSON file per scope (conversation, work item, global), merges them with the narrowest scope winning, drops records whose scope tags do not match the requested work item, and passes only cards that clear a no-model lexical overlap gate weighted by scope and recency. The immediately previous turn's conversation cards pass automatically on a follow-up.
advantages: Costs no model call and no network, survives restarts, fences work items from each other, and degrades quietly when a file is bad. Selected because: fixed in code
disadvantages: The gate is lexical, so a paraphrase sharing no word is missed. It is single-host and file based, and item-level ranking is covered only by unit tests, not by the metric.

name: In-memory thread-safe inbox
description: Holds a dictionary of per-conversation lists behind a lock inside the library's inbox module, satisfying the port with push, drain and peek. The orchestrator drains it between planner steps. Measured by plugging it into the live orchestrator and running synthetic cases where messages are pushed before or during a run, plus direct port-contract operations, with no model calls.
advantages: Simple, fast, thread-safe, and app-agnostic, so the same inbox serves chat, a frontend or anything else; the measurement checks delivery through the real planning loop and catches loss or cross-conversation leaks. Selected because: fixed in code
disadvantages: State is lost on restart and is not shared across processes or hosts, so a multi-process deployment needs a different implementation; the cases do not cover the deep retry boundary where a subprocess cannot be re-prompted.

name: Registry of built-in and host resolvers
description: A small protocol plus a registry mapping item type to resolver, with built-in note and file resolvers, coercion of plain callables into resolvers, and host entries overriding built-ins. Missing types render an unresolved-pointer line and errors return empty text.
advantages: Generic, with no host specifics, and a bad pointer cannot break assembly. Hosts add types without changing the library. Selected because: fixed in code
disadvantages: A silent empty result can hide a broken host resolver unless the unresolved line is noticed, and freshness depends entirely on the host's data layer.

name: Production registry under scripted host resolvers
description: Drives the real registry builder and the real card-content renderer with scripted host resolvers (objects, callables, raising, empty) and file text, checking unresolved lines for every type, budgets, item caps and abridged summaries.
advantages: Free, deterministic coverage of the shipped path including failure containment.
disadvantages: Host data layers are fakes, so real latency and error shapes are not tested.

name: Card repository with a cache seam and a null cache
description: The repository that talks to the card backend defines the cache protocol and the null cache, refreshes the listing in full or by delta, stores it after each success, offers failed writes to the cache, and serves the cached listing on a cold start during an outage while reporting degraded health.
advantages: Outages are visible but survivable, and correctness never depends on the cache.
disadvantages: The cache contract is narrow, so replay policy and conflict handling sit inside the repository, which makes it large and harder to reason about.

name: Durable file cache
description: Keeps a listing file and an outbox file in one directory, each written atomically through a temp file, with a lock for threads and swallowed I/O errors.
advantages: Survives restarts and crashes, so a cold start during an outage still serves cards and no queued write is lost. Selected because: core/selection_table.py cache-cards (default file)
disadvantages: Single-host only, so several hosts against one backend share nothing, and the file can go stale without notice.

name: No-op cache (shipped default of the seam)
description: Stores nothing and queues nothing, so every backend failure stays loud and nothing survives an outage. Used as the baseline against the live repository.
advantages: Zero state and zero risk of serving stale data, and the simplest behaviour to reason about.
disadvantages: Loses the listing and every failed write during an outage and cannot serve a cold start. Loses the listing and the outbox.

name: In-process memory cache
description: Keeps the last listing and a list of failed writes in process memory behind the same seam. It is an alternative that shows what a real cache buys.
advantages: Keeps cards and writes through a warm outage with no disk and trivial code.
disadvantages: Everything is lost on restart, so the cold-start case fails, and it is not shared across processes. Loses the listing and the outbox.

name: Durable file cache under outage scenarios
description: Plugs the file-backed cache into the same live repository in a temporary directory and runs the outage scenarios against an in-process card API, including a cold start while the backend is down.
advantages: The only arm that survives a process restart, so it is the one that passes the cold-start and lost-write cases.
disadvantages: Measures a single-host cache only, and a temporary directory hides real disk-full or permission problems. Single-host, so a card backend shared by several hosts has no shared cache.

name: Shipped deep-run prompt with standing instructions
description: Builds the real goal prompt, which includes the standing instructions as a required part, and runs it headless with every tool disabled, then has the model judge grade the stated plan.
advantages: Closest measured stand-in for what ships, so it is the arm that earns the selection even on a tie. Selected because: TIE, kept by the stated reason: the metric does not separate the standing instructions from the plain in-situ prompt (the pass rates are inside the leaderboard's margin for sampled, model-judged runs and the instructions spend more tokens), so the arm stays because quest_ai_runner/prompts/evolvable_structure.md is what the deep run actually loads (standing deep-run instructions, generated from the skill by scripts/sync_standing_instructions.py), and the arms without it are not what ships
disadvantages: Costs real model calls, spends extra tokens on the instructions, and scores only a described plan, not real edits.

name: In-situ prompt without the instruction layer
description: The same headless, tool-less deep-run path with the standing-instructions layer emptied, so the only difference from the shipped arm is the layer itself. It is a baseline.
advantages: Isolates the effect of the instruction layer cleanly and is cheaper in tokens.
disadvantages: It is not what ships, and the model may already behave well on many scenarios without help.

name: Chat-completion ablation with instructions
description: One plain model call per case with the instruction file as the system prompt, then the judge. It is an ablation that measures the instructions alone, outside the deep-run path.
advantages: Simple and cheap to run, and it separates the instruction text from the surrounding prompt.
disadvantages: A bare chat completion is not the setting the instructions ship in, so it should never be adopted on its own.

name: Chat-completion baseline without instructions
description: One call per case with a generic helpful-assistant system prompt, then the judge, so the gain from the instructions is a measured difference.
advantages: Cheapest comparator and gives a clear zero-instruction reference.
disadvantages: Not representative of the deep run, and a strong model may pass many cases without any help, which makes the gain look small.

name: Rubric-based model judge
description: A cheap-tier model call with tools off receives the scenario, expected behaviour, failure mode and reply, but never the regexes or reference replies, and returns a single JSON verdict. Unparseable output is a fail.
advantages: Grades behaviour in different words, resists vocabulary gaming, and generalises to new cases. Selected because: evaluation/components/esoi_behavior/judge.py (build_judge), used by every judged esoi_behavior arm
disadvantages: Can favour its own phrasing when it is the same model as the replies, costs a call per reply, and is only as good as the case author's rubric.

name: Regex-check floor
description: Passes a reply when every required pattern matches and no forbidden pattern does, with no model call. It is a baseline.
advantages: Free, instant and fully deterministic.
disadvantages: Agrees with the labels almost by construction since the same author wrote both, and it rewards the right words rather than the right action.

name: Package root with front doors
description: Imports the layers, installs the cross-layer wiring that keeps core independent of adapters and runner, and exposes version, config loading and a client front door that share one config file with a lane.
advantages: One import gives a consumer a documented, stable entry point and keeps layering clean.
disadvantages: Import-time wiring is global state, so order matters, and the exported name list must be maintained by hand.

name: Vendored edit-block parser
description: A modified, standard-library-only copy of an open-source tool's search-and-replace and whole-file edit parsing, with fuzzy matching tolerant of how models misformat edits (marker counts, filename placement, indent offsets).
advantages: Absorbs real model formatting errors that a fresh implementation would miss, with no outside dependency and licence terms respected.
disadvantages: It drifts from upstream, carries code the library did not design, and must be kept current by hand.

name: Long-lived background loop bridge
description: Runs coroutines and blocking work from synchronous adapter code on one lazily created daemon event loop, with a blocking call and a fire-and-forget call on a bounded executor.
advantages: Fixes the failure where an async client binds to the first loop and breaks later, so no consumer needs its own copy.
disadvantages: A single shared loop is a global resource and a long blocking task can delay others; it is invisible until misused.

name: Live package-surface driver
description: Imports the real package, checks names and registrations, calls the front doors in a scrubbed environment, runs the bridge, signature probes, strippers, report builders and edit parser, and imports modules in a subprocess whose sockets refuse.
advantages: Tests the promised surface exactly as a consumer meets it, with no model or network. Selected because: quest_ai_runner/__init__.py (the package root, load_config, load_client), core/async_bridge.py, core/signature_probe.py, core/scaffolding.py, bootstrap_email.py, vendor/
disadvantages: The name list is hand-written, so a new name is covered only once a case is added.

name: Minimal lane example
description: A short script that builds a config from a file and the environment and hands it to the shared lane driver, showing check, once and loop-forever modes.
advantages: Shows the smallest working lane and the contrast with hand-rolled drivers.
disadvantages: Hides detail by design, so customisation needs the second example and the docs.

name: Custom consumer configuration example
description: Builds a full runner configuration for an organisation entirely from environment variables with safe placeholders, covering model backend choice, corpus, deep-runner path and optional context settings.
advantages: A copyable reference for the many options of a real deployment, usable unchanged across environments.
disadvantages: Long and option-heavy, so a newcomer may be overwhelmed and the comments can go stale.

name: Example check harness
description: Compiles and imports each example, runs it as a subprocess in a scrubbed environment, calls the demo stub provider, loads the sample config, and checks index coverage and a secret and path scan.
advantages: Catches a broken or leaking example before a newcomer does, with no model or network. Selected because: examples/ as shipped (README.md lists each file)
disadvantages: Does not run demos that need a live backend or terminal to completion.

name: Task poller and claimer
description: Discovers due tasks per scan, deduplicates by signature across restarts, claims through the backend, hands each task to the executor with bounded concurrency, and pauses pickup when the host is overloaded.
advantages: Event-driven, restart-safe, and degrades instead of crashing on transient errors.
disadvantages: Large and stateful, with several guards that interact, so edge cases such as orphaned claims are hard to see.

name: Single-task executor
description: Runs one claimed task through the orchestrator and maps the result onto a status report: answer or met deep run is done, a short deep run is incomplete or failed, a decision is needs-you, a cancelled task gets no report. It never raises to the poller.
advantages: One clear unit of work that is easy to test with a mock client and stub brain.
disadvantages: The mapping from result to status is policy that must stay in step with the backend's status vocabulary.

name: Configured persona resolver
description: Chooses who runs a task from configuration, in order: a structured assignment field matching the registry, an optional model-judged explicit ask, then domain dominance, with optional auto-registration of unknown ids.
advantages: Replaces hand-written resolvers, needs no model call for structural lanes, and never activates on a bare name mention.
disadvantages: The judged and dominance steps depend on model judgement, and a wrong registry entry misroutes work.

name: Work-folder sync
description: Mirrors a work item's state and notes into a local file with runner-managed marked sections, and pushes new human notes back once, preserving human-authored text elsewhere in the file.
advantages: Idempotent, keeps human edits, and uses only the existing client methods.
disadvantages: A single shared file can conflict with hand edits near the markers, and direction rules must be respected by callers.

name: Shared lane entry point
description: Provides the check, once and loop-forever driver with argument parsing, env-file loading, local-time due gating and degrade-instead-of-crash behaviour on incomplete config.
advantages: Removes the duplicated glue each consumer used to write.
disadvantages: Consumers must fit its argv shape, and the local-time gate patches behaviour globally.

name: Offline lifecycle harness
description: Runs the real poller, executor, persona resolver, folder sync, scheduling helper and lane helpers against a fake client and a scripted model, with no model calls.
advantages: Deterministic and free coverage of the whole lifecycle including duplicates, lost claims and team scoping. Selected because: runner/config_wiring.py (a lane's run_lane drives Poller and TaskExecutor)
disadvantages: The fake client hides wire-level behaviour such as HTTP errors and real payload shapes, and crash recovery of orphaned claims is not yet covered.

name: Configuration dataclass and file entry point
description: The runner configuration dataclass declares every field, which of them a file may express, and the from-file constructor that hands the file to the loader. It is the single place where the set of settable fields lives, so adding a field and making it file-expressible happen together.
advantages: One typed object holds every setting, so consumers have a single contract and the file-expressible set cannot drift from the fields.
